title: Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) - Canadian SR&ED Glossary
description: Explore the relationship between Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) tax deductions and R&D assets in our Canadian SR&ED glossary.
summary: Capital cost allowance (CCA) in Canada intersects with SR&ED claims for depreciable property. Claimants claiming SR&ED capital property acquired after December 15, 2024 on Line 390 of Form T661 cannot also claim CCA on Schedule T2SCH8, while temporary 100% first-year CCA for qualifying manufacturing or processing buildings acquired on or after November 4, 2025 is proposed in Bill C-31 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 2), which had not received Royal Assent as of November 2026.

body.text: Capital cost allowance (CCA) in Canada intersects with SR&ED claims for depreciable property. Claimants claiming SR&ED capital property acquired after December 15, 2024 on Line 390 of Form T661 cannot also claim CCA on Schedule T2SCH8, while temporary 100% first-year CCA for qualifying manufacturing or processing buildings acquired on or after November 4, 2025 is proposed in Bill C-31 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 2), which had not received Royal Assent as of November 2026.

Canada's flagship federal innovation incentive—the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program—underwent its largest legislative expansion in over a decade upon the enactment of Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Effective retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024), enacted amendments to the federal Income Tax Act (ITA) double the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3.0 million to $6.0 million (raising the maximum annual federal cash refund from $1.05 million to $2.10 million), widen the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extend the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out ($15 million–$75 million) that Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) may also elect to apply, and restore eligibility for capital expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and qualifying equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024. Operationally, on April 1, 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Form T1322) enabling eligible businesses with under $25 million in annual gross business income to obtain upfront project eligibility determinations within eight weeks and halving post-filing expenditure review service standards from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days.

Three major prospective and sub-national shifts further shape Canadian R&D tax compliance in late 2026. First, in Federal Budget 2026 (Masters of Our Destiny, tabled November 5, 2026), the Department of Finance Canada proposed investing $930 million over five years to expand SR&ED eligible expenditures prospectively to encompass downstream commercialization, regulatory certification, and intellectual property (IP) registration and maintenance costs connected to eligible SR&ED projects—while omitting a preferential patent box tax-rate regime for the second consecutive federal budget, leaving Canada with no enacted or tabled federal patent box legislation. Second, among the provinces, Quebec replaced its legacy R&D wage, university, pre-competitive partnership, and consortium tax credits for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 with the consolidated, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Form RD-1029.8.CR) at 30% up to $1.0 million (less an exclusion threshold) and 20% on excess expenditures, while Ontario confirmed that depreciable capital property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 automatically qualifies for both the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) and the 3.5% non-refundable Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC). Third, within federal direct funding, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) replaced the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) with the Strategic Response Fund (SRF) and permanently closed the Net Zero Accelerator (NZA) stream to new applications as of November 4, 2025.
1. Statutory and Legislative Architecture of Canadian R&D Incentives
1.1 Primary Federal Statutory Provisions in the Income Tax Act and Regulations

Unlike discretionary government grants, Canada's federal SR&ED program is a statutory tax entitlement codified in the federal Income Tax Act, R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) and Part XXIX (Section 2900) of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945). Legislative policy and statutory drafting rest with the Department of Finance Canada, whereas technical review, financial audit, and tax credit disbursement are administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA).

The federal statutory architecture operates through two related but legally distinct calculations that corporate tax departments and auditors must evaluate sequentially. First, Section 37 of the Income Tax Act establishes a cumulative pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, permitting a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct allowable current and (post-December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED outlays when computing net business income in the current taxation year, or to carry unutilized pool balances forward indefinitely to future taxation years. Second, Section 127 and Section 127.1 govern the calculation, carryback, carryforward, recapture, and cash refundability of Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) earned on the claimant's pool of "qualified expenditures". Any federal SR&ED ITC deducted against Part I tax or refunded in cash in a taxation year is brought into the tax base in the following taxation year—reducing the claimant's Section 37 deductible expenditure pool or, where that pool is exceeded, entering taxable business income.

body.text: 1.2 Legislative Chronology from 2024 to Royal Assent of Bill C-15 in March 2026
Corporate tax compliance across 2024, 2025, and 2026 requires tracking five sequential legislative milestones that transformed initial policy proposals into binding statutory law:

items: December 16, 2024 — 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES): Released by the Department of Finance Canada on December 16, 2024, the 2024 Fall Economic Statement initially proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC from $3.0 million to $4.5 million, raising the CCPC prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extending the 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out, and restoring capital expenditure eligibility for property acquired (and lease costs incurred) after December 15, 2024. Draft legislative proposals reflecting the $4.5 million limit were released on August 15, 2025.

November 4, 2025 — Federal Budget 2025 (Canada Strong): Tabled in Parliament on November 4, 2025, Budget 2025 confirmed the government's intention to legislate the 2024 FES structural reforms while further raising the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced credit from the previously announced $4.5 million to $6.0 million, maintaining the retroactive effective date for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (statutorily expressed as taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024). Budget 2025 also introduced administrative reforms, including an upfront pre-claim approval mechanism effective April 1, 2026.

November 17–18, 2025 — Notice of Ways and Means Motion and Tabling of Bill C-15: A detailed Notice of Ways and Means Motion (NWMM) was tabled on November 17, 2025, followed on November 18, 2025 by First Reading of Bill C-15 (Budget Implementation Act, 2025, No. 1 / An Act to implement certain provisions of the budget tabled in Parliament on November 4, 2025).

February 23 & February 26, 2026 — Committee Amendments and Substantive Enactment: Minor amendments were adopted by the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance on February 23, 2026. Per EY's legislative tax analysis, Bill C-15 became substantively enacted for financial reporting purposes on February 26, 2026, when it passed third reading in the House of Commons.

March 26, 2026 — Royal Assent (S.C. 2026, c. 3): Bill C-15 received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Immediately following Royal Assent, the CRA updated its core SR&ED digital guidance on April 1, 2026, issued updated Form T661 (26), Form T1145, and Form T1146 on May 15, 2026, released revised Schedule T2SCH31 on May 22, 2026, and published revised Schedule T2SCH49 on May 29, 2026.

body.text: 1.3 Federal Budget 2026 Proposals and Status of the Promised Patent Box

On November 5, 2026, the Government of Canada released Federal Budget 2026: Masters of Our Destiny. Auditing Budget 2026 against prior fiscal announcements resolves two major policy questions for multinational and domestic tax planners.

First, Canada has not enacted or introduced a federal patent box regime. Although the 2024 Fall Economic Statement had promised details on a preferential patent box tax rate for IP commercialization income in the 2025 budget, both Budget 2025 (November 4, 2025) and Budget 2026 (November 5, 2026) omitted any patent box proposal or Notice of Ways and Means Motion, and as of November 2026 no bill establishing a patent box has been introduced in the 45th Parliament. Rather than taxing downstream IP royalty or embedded patent income at a reduced corporate rate, Budget 2025 directed programmatic funding to IP advisory services ($22.5 million for the Patent Collective and $75 million for the NRC IP Assist Program), while Budget 2026 opted to subsidize IP protection and commercialization outlays directly through the input-based SR&ED tax credit alongside proposed Patent Act amendments addressing ownership registration and anti-abuse demand-letter rules.

Second, Budget 2026 proposes investing approximately $930 million over five years (with ongoing support estimated at $235 million annually thereafter) to expand eligible expenditures under the SR&ED program to include certain commercialization expenses. Under Budget 2026 (pages 117 and 402–403), eligible SR&ED outlays would expand to include costs associated with bringing a new product or process to market—specifically obtaining necessary regulatory approvals or certifications and securing and maintaining intellectual property protection (registration and maintenance costs) in respect of IP developed during an eligible SR&ED project. General marketing or commercial expenses unconnected to an underlying qualifying SR&ED project remain ineligible. Qualifying commercialization and IP protection outlays will operate within the existing SR&ED rate framework (earning up to 35% for qualifying CCPCs/ECPCs and 15% otherwise), supported by forthcoming sector-specific CRA guidance. Tax practitioners note that these proposals remain subject to legislative enactment, applying prospectively to taxation years beginning on or after November 5, 2026 (2027 for calendar-year corporations) or expenses incurred on or after Budget Day once enacted.

Budget 2026 also proposes corporate compliance changes affecting SR&ED claimants. To reduce administrative friction, Budget 2026 eliminates the requirement to submit certified copies of board of directors' resolutions or officer authorizations to the CRA for designated corporate elections and agreements—explicitly including agreements for the allocation of qualified SR&ED expenditures and specified employee wages—effective for agreements made on or after Royal Assent of the implementing bill, although internal corporate records of authorizing resolutions must still be maintained. Conversely, for taxation years or fiscal periods ending after 2027, Budget 2026 proposes scaling fixed-dollar administrative penalties by entity size—imposing three times base penalty amounts on medium entities ($10 million–$50 million in related-group Canadian taxable capital for corporations, or $2 million–$10 million gross revenue for partnerships) and eight times base amounts on large entities exceeding those thresholds—alongside inflation adjustments and doubled penalties for repeated non-compliance across a three-year window.
2. Scientific and Technological Eligibility Framework
2.1 Subsection 248(1) Definition and Eligible Domains of Science and Technology

Technical eligibility across both the federal SR&ED program and harmonized provincial and territorial R&D tax credits is governed by the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Generally conforming to the OECD Frascati Manual within the natural sciences and engineering, subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis".

To qualify under subsection 248(1), activities must fall within one of four statutory categories: (1) basic research, undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; (2) applied research, undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; (3) experimental development, undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements; or (4) commensurate support work, strictly restricted to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research where such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of eligible basic research, applied research, or experimental development.

Other innovation activities outside those categories—including research in the social sciences or humanities, routine marketing, general administrative work, routine maintenance or quality control, purely commercial activities, and mineral/petroleum prospecting, exploration, or drilling (subject to specialized "specified sampling" exclusions in section 127 where mineral samples do not exceed 15 tonnes)—are excluded from SR&ED eligibility.
2.2 Defining SR&ED Projects and Separating Technological Uncertainty from Routine Problem-Solving

Under the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives and Guide T4088, technical reviews evaluate eligibility at the level of an SR&ED project. An SR&ED project comprises a set of interrelated activities that collectively are necessary to resolve defined scientific or technological uncertainties in attempting to achieve specific scientific or technological advancements, pursued through a systematic investigation or search by means of experiment or analysis performed by qualified individuals.

In audit practice, claimants must establish that simply solving complex business problems or improving a commercial product is insufficient. Scientific or technological uncertainty arises only where whether a technical objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it within system-level constraints, cannot be determined from standard engineering practice or publicly available scientific and technological knowledge. Once that technological uncertainty is established, the claimant must demonstrate a structured systematic investigation—formulating clear hypotheses, executing controlled experiments or formal analyses, recording empirical observations, and drawing logical conclusions as the work progresses. Where that systematic discipline is documented, a project qualifies for SR&ED even if the commercial prototype ultimately fails to meet market targets, because demonstrating why a hypothesized technical approach cannot overcome physical or computational constraints still generates a valid technological advancement.
3. Federal Tax Credit Rates, Expenditure Caps, Phase-Outs, and Refundability
3.1 Corporate Tax Context, Section 37 Pool Deductions, and Taxability of Relief

Evaluating the net benefit of SR&ED requires modelling the interaction between baseline Canadian corporate income tax rates, the Section 37 deduction pool, and Section 127 ITCs. Across 2024, 2025, and 2026, Canada's federal general corporate income tax rate remains unchanged at 15.0%, while qualifying CCPCs pay the 9.0% federal small-business rate on active business income up to the $500,000 small-business limit. Combined federal-provincial small-business corporate rates stand at 9.0% in Manitoba, 11.0% in Alberta and British Columbia, and 11.5% in New Brunswick, while combined general corporate income tax rates reach 26.5% in major R&D jurisdictions such as Quebec.

Allowable current and post-December 15, 2024 capital SR&ED expenditures enter the cumulative Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (subsection 37(1)), which a taxpayer may deduct immediately to shelter current-year taxable income or carry forward indefinitely to offset future profitable years. Crucially, SR&ED tax credits are themselves taxable. Any federal SR&ED ITC used to offset Part I tax or refunded in cash in a taxation year is included in taxable income in the following taxation year (via reduction of the following year's Section 37 pool, with any negative pool balance included in income). By contrast, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (and direct R&D grants) constitute government assistance in the current year—reducing both the current-year Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(d) and current-year Section 127 qualified expenditures under subsection 127(18), except that the portion of a provincial credit earned on the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) does not reduce the Section 37 pool and is instead included directly in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the taxation year received.
3.2 Enhanced 35% Versus Basic 15% Credit Rates, ECPC Eligibility, and De Facto Control

Federal SR&ED ITCs operate under a two-tier volume-based rate structure with no incremental spending floor. Under subsection 127(10.1), qualifying CCPCs and—for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) earn an enhanced 35% ITC (comprising the 15% basic rate plus a 20% statutory enhancement) on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to their annual expenditure limit of $6.0 million. Under subsection 127(9), the basic 15% ITC applies to qualified expenditures of CCPCs and ECPCs exceeding their expenditure limit, as well as to all qualified expenditures of foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries, non-eligible public corporations, individuals, trusts, and partnerships (subsection 127(8)).

To qualify as an ECPC under subsection 127(9) throughout a taxation year, a corporation must satisfy three cumulative statutory requirements: (1) it must be resident in Canada; (2) a class of its shares must be listed on a designated stock exchange per subsection 89(1) (such as the TSX, TSX Venture Exchange, CSE, or Cboe Canada—or the corporation must have elected, or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue, to be a public corporation); and (3) it must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. Canadian-resident subsidiaries in which all or substantially all of the shares are owned by one or more ECPCs also qualify for the refundable enhanced regime.

For venture-backed CCPCs and publicly traded ECPCs alike, the decisive legal audit threshold is control in fact (de facto control) under subsection 256(5.1) of the Income Tax Act. Beyond >50% voting share ownership (de jure control), the CRA evaluates whether non-resident shareholders, lenders, or commercial partners possess the clear right and ability to effect a significant change in the board of directors or exert dominant influence over strategic operations. Tax auditors examine six key de facto control factors: (1) rights to elect or remove a majority of directors and board nationality; (2) negative covenants or veto rights held by non-Canadian investors over IP licensing, asset disposals, or R&D budget pivots; (3) operational or management service agreements; (4) economic reliance on a single foreign lender, customer, or technology provider capable of forcing corporate decisions; (5) warrants, options, or convertible instruments conferring future voting control; and (6) direct non-Canadian involvement in routine or long-term business operations. In a documented venture-financing scenario where a Canadian technology company issues Class B shares with 40% voting rights to a foreign venture fund while granting that fund absolute veto power over IP licensing and R&D budget pivots, subsection 256(5.1) reclassifies the corporation as controlled in fact by non-residents—forfeiting access to the 35% refundable credit and dropping the firm to the 15% non-refundable rate.

body.text: (Audit Note on Draft Versus Enacted Straight-Line Phase-Out Slope: Practitioners reviewing transitional 2025 commentary should note that when the August 15, 2025 draft legislation proposed a $4.5 million expenditure limit phased out across the $60 million band from $15 million to $75 million, the reduction slope was $0.075 per dollar above $15 million. Once Budget 2025 and enacted Bill C-15 increased the expenditure limit to $6.0 million on a straight-line basis across the same $60 million band from $15 million to $75 million, the enacted straight-line formula reduces the $6.0 million expenditure limit by $0.10 for every $1.00 of prior-year Canadian taxable capital or three-year average gross revenue exceeding $15 million, reaching nil at $75 million.)

Under subsection 127(10.6), for standalone ECPCs (or electing standalone CCPCs), gross revenue is the annual revenue reported in the corporation's GAAP financial statements presented to shareholders averaged over the three preceding fiscal years ending before the current taxation year. Where a corporation belongs to a corporate group presenting consolidated financial statements, gross revenue is measured from the consolidated financial statements at the highest level of consolidation, and all group members must share a single $6.0 million expenditure limit (just as associated CCPCs must allocate their shared limit on Schedule T2SCH49 under subsections 127(10.21) and 127(10.3)). Short taxation years and multiple fiscal periods ending in a single calendar year require proration adjustments.

A worked comparison from Doane Grant Thornton illustrates the substantial cash-flow impact of the new CCPC gross revenue election. Suppose a CCPC has $45.0 million in prior-year Canadian taxable capital, $40.0 million in average annual gross revenue over the preceding three fiscal years, $500,000 in prior-year taxable income, and $4.5 million in current-year qualified SR&ED current expenditures:

items: Under Pre-Bill C-15 Law: With $45.0 million in taxable capital inside the old $10 million–$50 million phase-out, the CCPC's expenditure limit was compressed to $375,000, yielding just $131,250 in 35% refundable ITCs plus $618,750 in 15% non-refundable ITCs ($750,000 total federal ITCs).

Under Enacted Bill C-15 (Default Taxable Capital Method at $45.0M): Using prior-year taxable capital ($6.0M - [0.10 × ($45M - $15M)]), the expenditure limit would be $3.0 million, producing $1,050,000 in 35% refundable ITCs and $225,000 in 15% non-refundable ITCs ($1,275,000 total federal ITCs).

Under Enacted Bill C-15 (Electing the 3-Year Gross Revenue Method at $40.0M): By electing under subsection 127(10.31) to apply its $40.0 million three-year average gross revenue ($6.0M - [0.10 × ($40M - $15M)]), the CCPC raises its expenditure limit to $3.5 million, generating $1,225,000 in 35% cash-refundable ITCs plus $150,000 in 15% non-refundable ITCs ($1,375,000 total federal ITCs)—nearly a tenfold increase in immediate refundable cash compared to pre-Bill C-15 rules!

body.text: 3.4 Section 127.1 Refundability Matrix, Partnerships, Carryforwards, and Loss Restriction Events

When a taxpayer's federal Part I tax otherwise payable cannot absorb its earned SR&ED ITCs, Section 127.1 (subsections 127.1(1) to (3)) dictates whether the unclaimed balance is paid as a cash refund. Per the CRA's updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (October 7, 2026), statutory refundability depends on claimant classification and current versus capital expenditure nature:

cells: 1. CCPC that IS a Qualifying Corporation (and NOT an Excluded Corporation) (prior-year associated taxable income ≤ $500,000 and within taxable capital caps)
2. CCPC that is NOT a Qualifying Corporation (and NOT an Excluded Corporation) (e.g., prior-year taxable income > $500,000 or taxable capital > threshold)
3. Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) (taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024)
4. CCPC that IS a Qualifying Corporation, BUT ALSO an Excluded Corporation
5. Other Corporations (foreign-controlled subsidiaries, non-ECPC public corporations)
6. Unincorporated Individuals & Qualifying Trusts (where every beneficiary is a qualifying corporation or an individual other than a trust)
7. Partnerships (ITA s. 127(8)) (allocated only to active/general partners; specified/limited partners excluded)
0% to corporate partners (even if the partner is a CCPC!)

body.text: Three structural tax-planning rules govern partnerships, carryovers, and corporate reorganizations. First, under subsection 127(8), partnerships compute SR&ED ITCs strictly at the 15% basic rate, cannot utilize subsection 127(13) non-arm's-length expenditure transfers, cannot allocate SR&ED ITCs to "specified members" (passive or limited partners not regularly, continuously, and substantially engaged in the partnership's active business), and cannot treat payments to partners as eligible SR&ED salaries because a partner cannot be an employee of the partnership. Crucially, even where an active partner is a CCPC, the allocated partnership SR&ED ITC remains at 15% and none of it is refundable to the CCPC (subsections 127(8), 127.1(2), 127.1(2.01)).

Second, under subsection 127(5), any non-refunded SR&ED ITC balance may be carried back 3 taxation years (capped at Part I tax otherwise payable in that prior year after accounting for any ITC refunded in that prior year) or carried forward 20 taxation years. Under subsection 127.1(3), any SR&ED ITC refunded in cash is deemed to have been deducted against Part I tax in the year and reduces the ITC pool available for carryback or carryforward.

Third, while corporate amalgamations (Section 87, paragraphs 87(2)(j.6), (l), (qq)) and wind-ups (Section 88, paragraphs 88(1)(e.2), (e.3)) preserve SR&ED expenditure pools and ITC carryforwards, an acquisition of control triggers a loss restriction event (subsection 251.2(2)) and a deemed taxation year-end (subsection 249(4)). Under paragraphs 127(9)(j) and (k) and subsections 127(9.1) and (9.2), unused ITC carryforwards and carrybacks across a loss restriction event are restricted to offsetting tax payable derived from carrying on that same business or a business where substantially all income derives from similar properties or services.
4. Qualifying Expenditures and Overhead Calculation Methodologies
4.1 Proxy Method Versus Traditional Method Election

body.text: Most Canadian claimants elect the Proxy Method because earning a fixed 55% notional overhead uplift on directly engaged technical salaries eliminates the compliance burden of tracking invoice-level overhead while permitting actual rent, utilities, and general computing costs to be deducted as ordinary business expenses. Conversely, the Traditional Method benefits claimants whose actual incremental SR&ED overhead (such as dedicated pilot-plant utilities, specialized cloud/compute outlays, or incremental clerical/administrative support on Line 360) exceeds 55% of directly engaged technical wages. Under Section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations and CRA overhead policy, any overhead or administrative expense claimed on Line 360 under the Traditional Method must satisfy a strict two-part "directly attributable" test: (1) it must be directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, and (2) it must be incremental—meaning the cost would not have been incurred had the SR&ED prosecution not occurred.
4.2 Salaries and Wages, Specified Employees, YMPE Caps, Unpaid Remuneration, and Foreign SR&ED

Under subsection 248(1) and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), "salary or wages" means employment income from an office or employment computed under Subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Income Tax Act (excluding superannuation or pension benefits, retiring allowances, and partnership income distributions). Eligibility depends strictly on the technical tasks performed rather than job titles. Only the portion of an employee's salary reasonably relating to SR&ED is allowable; however, under the statutory All or Substantially All (ASA) rule (subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)), if 90% or more of an employee's working time in the taxation year is devoted to prosecuting SR&ED, 100% of their eligible salary is treated as an allowable SR&ED expenditure, subject to specified employee caps.

For specified employees (clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B), subsections 37(9) and 37(9.1)), strict statutory caps prevent owner-managers and non-arm's-length shareholders from shifting corporate profits into subsidized SR&ED payroll. First, a specified employee's allowable SR&ED salary is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under Section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan, prorated for the number of days in the year the individual was a specified employee. (Audit Note: Although Canada introduced a second earnings ceiling—the Year's Additional Maximum Pensionable Earnings, or YAMPE—for CPP2 contributions starting in 2024, the statutory Section 37 SR&ED formula remains tied strictly to the first ceiling, YMPE, not YAMPE.) Second, under subsection 37(9), all bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to specified employees are excluded from SR&ED expenditures. Third, when computing the 55% PPA salary base under the Proxy Method, specified employees are restricted to 75% of allowable salary (capped at statutory YMPE-linked limits), and specified employee taxable benefits are excluded from the PPA base. Fourth, under subsections 37(9.2) to 37(9.4), no SR&ED wages may be claimed for a specified employee working for two or more associated corporations unless the group files Form T1174 allocating the single 5 × YMPE ceiling across the associated corporations.

body.text: Two additional timing and territorial rules govern SR&ED payroll audits. Under subsection 78(4) (the 180-day unpaid remuneration rule), any accrued employee salary or remuneration remaining unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which it was incurred is deemed not incurred in that taxation year, becoming claimable only in the subsequent year when paid (reasonable vacation/holiday pay and statutory salary deferral arrangement amounts are deemed paid on day 180 for Section 37 purposes, but cannot enter the PPA salary base). Under subsections 37(1.4), 37(1.5), and 37(2), permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work carried on outside Canada by Canadian employees is capped at 10% of total SR&ED salaries and wages incurred for SR&ED performed inside Canada (reported on Line 306 of Form T661, and split between non-specified employees on Line 307 and specified employees on Line 309 such that Line 309 Limit = (10% of Line 306) - Line 307).
4.3 Subcontractors, Non-Arm's-Length Transfers, Third-Party Payments, and Materials

Payments under arm's-length Canadian SR&ED contracts—where a contractor performs basic research, applied research, experimental development, or support work in Canada on the claimant's behalf and the claimant receives the rights to the SR&ED—are 100% deductible in the Section 37 pool (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i)), but only 80% of the eligible contract expenditure qualifies for Section 127 ITCs (subsection 127(9)). The geographic test turns on where the SR&ED work was physically performed, not where the contractor is incorporated; work performed outside Canada under a subcontract is ineligible. Conversely, to prevent double-dipping by both payer and performer, the arm's-length Canadian performer must deduct the "contract payment" received or receivable from its own qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsections 127(9) and 127(18) before computing any ITC of its own.

Where SR&ED is subcontracted between non-arm's-length corporations, contract payments do not directly qualify for ITCs in the payer's hands; instead, under subsection 127(13), the performing corporation and related payer may jointly file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, updated May 15, 2026) to transfer the performer's underlying qualified expenditures to the payer, with the performer reporting the transferred sum on Line 540 of Form T661. Similarly, non-arm's-length parties allocate SR&ED assistance using Form T1145 (updated May 15, 2026).

Third-party payments (subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.01) to (iii)) made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or resident Canadian R&D corporations for SR&ED carried out in Canada are likewise 100% deductible in Section 37 and 80% eligible for Section 127 ITCs, provided the SR&ED relates to a business of the claimant (paragraph 37(8)(c)) and the claimant acquires the entitlement to exploit the results (distinct from owning the SR&ED outright as in a contract). Agricultural producers contributing check-off dues or cash through agricultural organizations that fund approved SR&ED entities and retain preferential exploitation rights may also claim their allocated percentage on Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND). Direct materials consumed or materials transformed in performing SR&ED qualify at 100% for both Section 37 deduction and Section 127 ITCs under both the Proxy and Traditional methods.
4.4 Reinstated Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment, Lease Costs, and ITC Recapture

Eliminated since January 1, 2014, capital expenditures and qualifying equipment lease costs were restored by Bill C-15 for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 and lease costs first incurred/payable after December 15, 2024, governed by the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), and SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026).

To qualify as dedicated SR&ED capital property on Line 390 of Form T661 (once available for use), depreciable machinery, laboratory apparatus, test rigs, or high-performance AI/computing hardware acquired after December 15, 2024 must be acquired with the intention either to: (1) use all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time over its expected useful life in performing SR&ED in Canada, or (2) consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value in performing SR&ED in Canada. Capital outlays claimed on Line 390 cannot also be claimed for Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) on Schedule T2SCH8. Crucially, while both new and used depreciable property meeting this 90% test qualify for immediate Section 37 income deduction, depreciable property that has been used in any manner prior to its SR&ED use does NOT qualify for any SR&ED ITCs—only new property earns the 15% or 35% (up to 40% cash refundable) ITC. Land, buildings, leasehold interests, and rights to use buildings remain excluded from SR&ED capital incentives. (Separate CCA Planning Note: Outside SR&ED, Budget 2025 proposed, and Bill C-31 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 2, still before Parliament as of November 2026) would implement, temporary 100% first-year CCA immediate expensing for qualifying Canadian manufacturing or processing buildings acquired on or after November 4, 2025 and first used before 2030 where ≥90% of floor space is used for manufacturing or processing, stepping down to 75% in 2030–2031 and 55% in 2032–2033.)

Where new depreciable equipment acquired after December 15, 2024 falls below the 90% threshold because it splits operating time between SR&ED and commercial production, claimants may still earn a partial SR&ED ITC under the reinstated Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) rules (subsection 127(9), reported on Line 504 of Form T661) if the asset is used primarily (more than 50% of the time) for SR&ED in Canada across statutory first-term and second-term periods. For software and AI companies electing the Proxy Method, this capital restoration creates an important compute-procurement trade-off: rented cloud compute is absorbed into the fixed 55% salary PPA without generating incremental ITCs, whereas purchasing new on-premises GPU/HPC servers dedicated ≥90% to SR&ED generates an extra 35% federal ITC (40% refundable) plus applicable Ontario or Quebec capital credits on top of the 55% salary PPA. Finally, if SR&ED capital property is later sold or converted to commercial use, recapture rules (subsections 127(27) to 127(36), computed on Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND)) recover previously claimed tax benefits across CCA, unclaimed SR&ED capital pools, and SR&ED ITCs.
5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes
5.1 Master Comparison of All Thirteen Canadian Jurisdictions

Nine provinces and Yukon supplement federal SR&ED with sub-national R&D tax credits; Prince Edward Island, Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not offer R&D tax credits. Except for Quebec (administered by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration — TRA), all provincial and territorial credits are administered by the CRA alongside the T2 corporate return.

body.text: 5.2 Quebec: Consolidation into the Refundable CRIC Regime (Post-March 25, 2025)

In its 2025–2026 Provincial Budget (tabled March 25, 2025), Quebec overhauled its R&D tax system by replacing four legacy R&D tax credits—the R&D Salaries and Wages Credit (Form RD-1029.7-V, previously 30% on the first $3.0 million for SMEs with <$50 million global assets phasing down to 14% at $75 million, above a $50,000–$225,000 exclusion threshold), the University/Public Research Centre Credit (Form RD-1029.8.6-V), the Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research Credit (Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V), and the Research Consortium Fees Credit (Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V), alongside abolishing the Technological Adaptation Services Credit—with the unified, 100% refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), effective for taxation years or fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025. Under transitional rules, taxation years beginning before March 26, 2025 continue under the legacy forms (with Form RD-222-V), cumulative research consortium fee balances at the end of a taxation year ending after March 25, 2025 remain claimable on Form RD-1029.8.9.03-V for taxation years ending on or before December 31, 2029, and the Ministère de l'Économie, de l'Innovation et de l'Énergie (MEIE) continues issuing public research centre and consortium recognition certificates for CRIC purposes.

Per official Revenu Québec and Gouvernement du Québec guidance, whereas legacy Quebec R&D credits were open to individuals and trusts, the CRIC may only be claimed by corporations operating a business in Quebec with an establishment in Quebec (directly or as corporate members of a qualified partnership, although partnership allocations are ineligible for the 30% enhanced tier; note that while one general tax table included individuals under the 20% column, Revenu Québec explicitly restricts post-March 25, 2025 claims to corporations). Crucially, the CRIC expands Quebec's tax base beyond core R&D to include pre-commercialization activities performed in Quebec in direct continuity with R&D conducted in Quebec by or on behalf of the corporation (such as industrial design, prototyping, regulatory testing, and product validation), as well as capital property acquisition costs for brand-new depreciable equipment used in Quebec almost exclusively (≥90%) in eligible R&D or pre-commercialization (excluding land, buildings, rights to use buildings/land, and property under a Large Investment Project tax holiday). Eligible CRIC expenditures encompass 100% of Quebec R&D/pre-commercialization employee wages (including direct support staff), 50% of arm's-length Quebec subcontracts, 50% of payments to eligible Quebec universities, public research centres, or research consortia, and 100% of eligible new equipment acquisitions.

To focus assistance on higher-value-added jobs, a corporation's net qualified CRIC expenditures must exceed an annual exclusion threshold equal to the greater of: (1) $50,000 (prorated for short taxation years under 51 weeks), or (2) the sum across participating employees of the Quebec personal income tax basic personal amount ($18,571 in 2025), prorated by the time each employee devotes to eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities. Per Gouvernement du Québec rules, CRIC pays 30% on qualified expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold up to the $1,000,000 ceiling (shared among associated corporations, meaning at a $50,000 threshold on $1,000,000 of eligible spend, $950,000 × 30% = $285,000 cash refund, with RCGT's practitioner guide noting the 30% tier applies to Canadian-controlled corporations while some budget summaries describe the 30% band as up to $1.0 million above the threshold) and 20% on all qualified expenditures exceeding $1,000,000—raising Quebec's base rate for large R&D spenders from 14% to 20% regardless of global asset size! Claims are filed on Form RD-1029.8.CR (RD-1029.8.CR-T) with the CO-17 return. (Quebec also concurrently revised its E-Business Tax Credit—CDAE—to cover AI data processing and hosting while excluding maintenance/evolution activities.)
5.3 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, OBRITC, and 2026 Capital Expenditure Harmonization

Ontario administers three corporate R&D credits under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), each requiring an Ontario permanent establishment, SR&ED performed in Ontario, and filing of federal Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31. First, official Ontario Ministry of Finance guidance on ontario.ca for the ORDTC and the 2026 Ontario Economic Outlook and Fiscal Review (Annex: Enhancing Support Through Ontario's Research and Development Tax Credits, published October 29, 2026) confirm that Ontario's statutory cross-reference to federal section 127 automatically restored capital expenditure eligibility for both the OITC and ORDTC upon Bill C-15's Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, effective for depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 (despite a lagging update on Ontario's general OITC webpage as of October 30, 2026; Ontario estimates this adds over $50 million in support over three years across roughly 700 businesses, while capital acquired from January 1, 2014 to December 15, 2024 remains excluded).

Second, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566) pays an 8% fully refundable credit on up to $3.0 million of qualified Ontario expenditures (up to $240,000 cash, phasing out across $500,000–$800,000 of taxable income or $25 million–$50 million of Canadian taxable paid-up capital, with waiver authority under subsection 96(14)). Third, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508) provides an uncapped 3.5% non-refundable credit (3-year carryback / 20-year carryforward) open to all corporations, calculated after deducting OITC from the Ontario expenditure base, and subject to a 23.56% Ontario recapture rate if claimed capital property is sold or converted to commercial use. Loss-making startups may file a written ORDTC waiver within six months of tax year-end (or on an amended return) to prevent unusable non-refundable ORDTC from grinding down their 35% cash-refundable federal SR&ED pool. Fourth, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Schedules 568 & 569) provides a 20% fully refundable credit on up to $20 million annually (up to $4.0 million cash/year) for eligible R&D contracts with Ontario universities, colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, or Ontario Centres of Excellence.
5.4 Western, Atlantic, and Territorial Regimes

In Western Canada, British Columbia (Form T666, strict 18-month filing deadline) provides a 10% SR&ED credit—100% refundable for CCPCs and, for tax years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, ECPCs up to the federal expenditure limit of $6.0 million in qualified BC expenditures ($600,000 maximum cash), and non-refundable (3-year carryback / 10-year carryforward) above that limit or for other corporations. For a qualifying BC CCPC claiming $100,000 of directly engaged salary under the Proxy Method ($155,000 gross base including the 55% PPA), the 10% refundable BC credit yields $15,500 cash and reduces the federal base to $139,500, earning 35% × $139,500 = $48,825 federal cash—totalling $64,325, or 64.33% of eligible salary recovered in cash (matching the ~64% figure cited by BC SR&ED practitioners)! Alberta's Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) (AT1 Schedule 29 and Form AT4970, filed within 15 months after the AT1 filing due date) pays a 100% refundable credit on up to $4.0 million in annual Alberta R&D spending (phased out across $10 million–$50 million in taxable capital), structured as 8% up to the corporation's two-year rolling average Alberta R&D spend and 20% on incremental spending above that two-year average. Saskatchewan (T2SCH403) offers 10% refundable on the first $1.0 million for CCPCs and 10% non-refundable (3-year carryback / 10-year carryforward) otherwise, while Manitoba (T2SCH380, due 1 year after the filing due date) provides a 15% credit that is half refundable (7.5% cash / 7.5% non-refundable, 20-year carryforward) for in-house R&D and 100% refundable (15%) for R&D contracted to qualifying institutes.

Across Atlantic and Northern Canada, New Brunswick (T2SCH360), Nova Scotia (T2SCH340, 18-month deadline), and Newfoundland and Labrador (T2SCH301 for corporations / Form T1129 for individuals, due 12 months after the filing due date) each provide an uncapped 15% fully refundable R&D tax credit, while Yukon offers an uncapped 15% fully refundable R&D credit plus an additional 5% refundable credit (20% total) on R&D payments to Yukon University.
6. Direct R&D Grants, Federal Innovation Ecosystem, and Stacking Mechanics
6.1 NRC IRAP, Strategic Response Fund (Replacing SIF and NZA), and Federal Funding Pillars

Canadian innovators routinely pair retrospective SR&ED claims with upfront direct contributions, led for SMEs by the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP). Operating for over 75 years without an open online application portal, NRC IRAP delivers advisor-driven, non-repayable cost-shared R&D reimbursements through Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs) to incorporated, for-profit Canadian SMEs with 500 or fewer full-time equivalent employees (excluding sole proprietorships, general partnerships, ULCs/LLCs, and non-profits from leading projects). While typical SME awards are scaled to project readiness (such as $100,000 to $1.0 million under IRAP's Clean Technology stream, reported by funding trackers to be mid-transition in 2026), IRAP's Large Value Contribution stream reaches up to $10 million per firm, having directed $76 million across 72 SMEs in 2024–25. Meanwhile, the Canada Innovation Corporation (CIC)—incorporated in February 2023 under the Canada Development Investment Corporation (CDEV) with a $1.0 billion five-year mandate—is scheduled per CDEV's 2026–2030 Corporate Plan (published June 2026) to achieve full implementation no later than 2026–2027.

For large-scale industrial R&D and capital deployment, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED)—which disbursed $4.34 billion in net spending in 2025–26, including $1.005 billion under the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF), $567.7 million for the Canada Foundation for Innovation, $335.6 million for Global Innovation Clusters, $125.2 million for Mitacs Inc., $115.7 million for AI Compute Infrastructure, and $64.4 million for the Canadian Quantum Champions Program—executed a major program pivot in late 2025. Specifically, ISED sunset and permanently closed the Net Zero Accelerator (NZA) to new applications on November 4, 2025 due to declining demand and overlap (driving $723.8 million in planned 2026–27 spending reductions per ISED's 2026–27 Departmental Plan), and replaced SIF with the Strategic Response Fund (SRF). According to practitioner analyses of ISED's SRF guidelines and Budget 2026 commentary, the SRF carries an envelope of up to $5 billion (plus a $1.0 billion six-year recapitalization announced in Budget 2026), requires minimum total project costs of $20 million+ and federal contributions of $10 million+ (~50% blended repayable/non-repayable cost-sharing), drops NZA's decarbonization mandate, and targets advanced manufacturing, AI compute, semiconductors, defence and dual-use technologies, critical minerals, aerospace, biomanufacturing, and tariff-impacted trade-resilience projects. Parallel capital incentives include Canada's refundable Clean Economy Investment Tax Credits—including the CCUS ITC (full rates extended through 2035 in Budget 2025), Clean Hydrogen ITC (expanded to methane pyrolysis), and Clean Technology (up to 30%) and Clean Electricity (15%) ITCs (both proposed in Budget 2026 to extend through 2040).
6.2 Government Assistance Rules and End-to-End Multi-Tier Stacking Models

Under ITA paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18), direct government grants (such as NRC IRAP or Scale AI contributions) and provincial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance that reduces the federal qualified expenditure pool before the 35% or 15% federal ITC is computed. Consequently, headline grant and tax credit percentages never sum linearly, and assistance interactions must be modelled sequentially from direct grants to provincial credits to federal SR&ED.

Worked Multi-Tier Stacking Audit Model (2026 Taxation Year — Qualifying Ontario CCPC): Consider a qualifying Ontario CCPC (under $15 million taxable capital and under $500,000 prior-year taxable income) incurring $1,340,000 in out-of-pocket Ontario R&D outlays in calendar year 2026 under the Proxy Method, while receiving a $250,000 NRC IRAP contribution toward current R&D costs:

$1,000,000 salaries + $550,000 PPA (55% × $1M salaries) + $160,000 contractor (80% × $200K) + $40,000 materials + $100,000 new capital (ITA s. 127(9))
Subtract $250,000 government assistance from current R&D pool (ITA s. 127(18))

body.text: Under Section 37 of the Income Tax Act, the SR&ED reporting deadline is strictly 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax filing due date, with zero administrative extension authority: (1) for corporations (T2), 6 months after tax year-end plus 12 months equals 18 months after the corporation's tax year-end (e.g., a December 31, 2025 year-end has a T2 due date of June 30, 2026 and an absolute SR&ED deadline of June 30, 2027); (2) for individuals carrying on business (T1), June 15 of the second following calendar year (12 months after the June 15 T1 due date); and (3) for trusts (T3), 12 months after the 90-day post-year-end T3 due date. If prescribed T661/Schedule 31 fields are missing after the reporting deadline passes, the CRA cannot accept late information and the SR&ED claim is permanently disallowed; the CRA therefore recommends filing at least 90 days before the reporting deadline. By contrast, where third-party claim preparer disclosures in Part 9 of Form T661 (including preparer name, Business Number or Social Insurance Number collected under ITA s. 237, and fee arrangement) are incomplete, inaccurate, or missing, subsections 162(5.1) to 162(5.3) impose a $1,000 penalty per claim on the taxpayer and preparer, without disqualifying the underlying Section 37 expenditure deduction.
7.2 CRA Elective Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026) and Service Standards

Launched on April 1, 2026, the CRA's optional Pre-Claim Approval Process allows qualifying businesses—CCPCs, Canadian corporations, and Canadian partnerships operating in Canada that are in good standing with the CRA and have less than $25 million in annual gross business income—to obtain upfront project eligibility determinations before beginning work or incurring costs, provided the proposed projects do not involve issues currently under objection or litigation.
The application follows four sequential steps:

items: Request a Case Number: Submit a brief web request on Canada.ca; existing SR&ED claimants receive a case number in My Business Account within 2 business days, while new claimants receive a CRA phone call within 5 business days.
Submit Form T1322 in My Business Account: File Form T1322 (Application for SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval) for up to 3 planned projects, attaching existing project plans and technical documentation.

Meet with a CRA SR&ED Specialist: Within 4 weeks of application, new SR&ED claimants attend a mandatory technical meeting with an SR&ED specialist, while existing claimants in good standing may be contacted if clarification is needed.

Receive Official Determination and File Post-Work Claim: Within 8 weeks of completing the My Business Account submission, the CRA issues an official determination valid for up to 3 years (if declined, the business may still submit a standard SR&ED claim after performing the work, and approved claimants must still file Form T661 and Schedule 31 annually to claim actual expenditures).

body.text: Under the CRA's 2026 processing timeframes for refundable claims (non-refundable claims carry no service standard), claims accepted as filed are processed within 60 calendar days; refundable claims selected for expenditure review that only include pre-approved projects are processed within 90 calendar days (cutting review times in half); and refundable claims selected for review containing any non-pre-approved project or any project materially differing from its pre-approved scope are processed within 180 calendar days. First-time filers (or those with no claim in the prior three years) may also be selected for the mandatory First-Time Claimant Advisory Service, and all claimants are guided by The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (which replaced The SR&ED Technical Review: A Guide for Claimants in 2026).
8. Jurisprudence, CRA Audit Standards, and Dispute Resolution
8.1 Landmark Tax Court and Federal Court of Appeal Precedents

Canadian courts interpret subsection 248(1) through a settled line of binding appellate jurisprudence anchored in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. R. (1998, Tax Court of Canada). Northwest Hydraulic established the foundational multi-criterion test governing whether claimed activities constitute SR&ED rather than routine engineering: (1) existence of a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty that cannot be resolved by standard practice; (2) formulation of specific hypotheses aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty; (3) adoption of procedures according with the systematic discipline of the scientific method, including formulating, testing, and modifying hypotheses; (4) pursuit of a technological advancement; and (5) maintenance of contemporaneous records of hypotheses tested and results achieved as the work progressed.

The Federal Court of Appeal formally adopted and entrenched the Northwest Hydraulic test in R I S - Christie Ltd. v. Canada ([1999] 1 C.T.C. 132, FCA) and CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393, alongside Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd.). Most notably, in National R&D Inc. v. Canada (2022 FCA 72), the taxpayer challenged the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion—arguing that strict adherence to the scientific method and hypothesis formulation lacked a textual foundation in subsection 248(1) and pointing to the CRA's updated 2021 administrative guidelines. The Federal Court of Appeal rejected that argument and reaffirmed Northwest Hydraulic in full—a precedent consistently enforced in subsequent Tax Court of Canada rulings such as Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023).
8.2 Contemporaneous Documentation Standards, Audit Defence, and Statutory Appeals

To substantiate an SR&ED review conducted by a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and Financial Reviewer (FR), documentation must establish what work was done, who was involved, when it was performed, and how expenditures were calculated. While dated, signed project-specific records carry the highest evidentiary weight, the CRA accepts diverse contemporaneous artefacts generated naturally during R&D execution: whiteboard drawings, test protocols, raw test data, analytical results and conclusions, final project reports, photographs and videos, physical prototypes, samples, scrap and scrap records, resource allocation logs, activity records and employee timesheets separating SR&ED from non-SR&ED hours, payroll records, contracts and lease agreements, purchase invoices, accounting ledgers, and proof of payment. Senior technical and financial personnel with direct knowledge of the R&D should participate directly in CRA virtual or on-site review meetings.
Where disputes arise during or after a CRA review, claimants follow a four-step administrative and judicial resolution pathway:

items: Direct Reviewer Resolution: Address draft technical or financial review findings directly with the assigned Research and Technology Advisor and/or Financial Reviewer before final issuance of the review report.

Managerial Escalation: Escalate unresolved audit or procedural concerns to the Research and Technology Manager and/or Financial Review Manager in accordance with the CRA's Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns.

Formal Notice of Objection: File a formal objection with the CRA within 90 calendar days from the date of the Notice of assessment or Notice of reassessment (noting that Budget 2026 has proposed prospectively extending objection timeframes once legislated, and that enacted Budget 2024 "stop the clock" rules suspend reassessment limitation periods whenever a taxpayer seeks judicial review of a CRA audit requirement or notice).

Judicial Appeal: If the claimant disagrees with the CRA's decision on the objection, file a formal judicial appeal to the Tax Court of Canada, with further appellate review on questions of law before the Federal Court of Appeal.
